content: The fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) refers to the proportion or percentage of oxygen present in the air being measured. In clinical settings, patients experiencing respiratory distress are often provided with oxygen-enriched air, which has a higher oxygen concentration than the atmospheric level. The atmospheric FiO2 is approximately 21%, while 100% oxygen corresponds to an FiO2 of 1.0. In medical practice, FiO2 is carefully regulated, even during mechanical ventilation, to prevent oxygen toxicity. FiO2 is commonly used in medicine to represent the percentage of oxygen involved in gas exchange within the lungs. It is important to note that while FiO2 may remain constant, changes in barometric pressure can alter the partial pressure of oxygen. The partial pressures of oxygen in alveolar gas (PAO2), expired gas (PEO2), and inspired gas (PiO2) are key parameters in respiratory physiology. The ratio of physiologic dead space to tidal volume (VD/VT) is also an important consideration in assessing ventilation efficiency. In medical contexts, FiO2 is the assumed percentage of oxygen concentration participating in gas exchange within the alveoli. This parameter is critical for evaluating respiratory function and oxygenation. The ratio of arterial oxygen partial pressure (PaO2) to FiO2 is a widely used indicator of hypoxemia, as defined by the American-European Consensus Conference on lung injury. A high FiO2 can influence the PaO2/FiO2 ratio, which is a key metric in assessing oxygenation status. The PaO2/FiO2 ratio, also known as the Carrico index, compares the oxygen level in arterial blood to the oxygen concentration being inhaled. This ratio is used to evaluate the efficiency of oxygen transfer from the lungs to the blood. To measure this, a sample of arterial blood is collected. A PaO2/FiO2 ratio of ≤200 mmHg is a diagnostic criterion for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) according to the AECC criteria. The more recent Berlin criteria classify mild ARDS as a ratio of <300 mmHg, which may indicate the need for inpatient treatment. Additionally, a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of ≤333 mmHg is one of the variables included in the SMART-COP risk score, which predicts the need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support in patients with community-acquired pneumonia.
